# Square-root concavity of tails of a concave integer sequence

This is a scalar strengthening of the previously proved log-concave-sequence
integer-mean tail bound. It is not a mixed-dimensional center theorem.

Let (a_k)_(k=l)^r be a finite strictly positive concave sequence: its
successive differences are nonincreasing. Normalize sum a_k=1 and write
F_i=sum_(k=i)^r a_k. Then the sequence sqrt(F_i), i=l,...,r, is concave.
The terminal value F_(r+1)=0 is NOT included in this assertion.

Proof. It suffices to check an index l<i<r. Set

    F=F_i, A=a_(i-1), B=a_i.

If A<=B, then F_(i-1)+F_(i+1)=2F+A-B<=2F, and concavity and monotonicity
of the square root give the result.

Suppose instead A=B+delta with delta>0. Concavity of a implies

    a_(i+j)<=B-j delta for every existing j>=0.

Since i<r and a_(i+1)>0, one has B>delta. Put q=B/delta and write
q=m+rho, where m=floor(q) and 0<=rho<1. Extending the upper bound by its
positive part beyond the support gives

 F <= delta sum_(j>=0) (q-j)_+
   = (delta/2)[q(q+1)+rho(1-rho)]
   <= B(B+delta)/(2 delta)+delta/8.                    (1)

(The displayed sum formula includes the integer case rho=0.) Because
F>=B>delta, squaring the following inequalities is legitimate. The desired

    2 sqrt(F)>=sqrt(F+B+delta)+sqrt(F-B)

is equivalent, after squaring twice, to

    2 delta F<=B(B+delta)+delta^2/4,

which is precisely (1). This proves the sequence concavity.

## Closed tails at an integer mean

If the mean m=sum k a_k is an integer, then

    sum_(k>=m) a_k >=4/9,
    sum_(k<=m) a_k >=4/9.                             (2)

For a singleton support this is immediate. Otherwise m lies strictly
between l and r. Interpolate sqrt(F_i) linearly between consecutive
integer indices. The proved concavity and Jensen give

    sqrt(F_m)>=sum_i a_i sqrt(F_i).

Since a_i=F_i-F_(i+1), the last sum is the upper-endpoint Riemann sum
for the increasing function sqrt(t) over the partition by the tail
values F_i, including F_(r+1)=0 only as an integration endpoint. Hence

    sum_i a_i sqrt(F_i)>=integral_0^1 sqrt(t)dt=2/3.

Squaring proves the upper-tail bound; reflection proves the lower-tail
bound. Notice that no concavity at the artificial zero endpoint is used.

The constant 4/9 is sharp as an infimum. For any positive integer k, use
indices j=0,...,3k and unnormalized masses

    a_j=3k+1-j.

Their total is (3k+1)(3k+2)/2, and their mean is exactly k. The upper
closed tail at k has normalized mass

    (2k+1)(2k+2)/[(3k+1)(3k+2)],

which tends to 4/9 as k tends to infinity.

## Mixed interpretation with one continuous coordinate

For a convex body in R x R, its positive interval-fiber lengths form a
concave sequence on their consecutive integer support. Therefore, if
its actual mixed-volume centroid has an integer first coordinate, every
vertical closed halfspace containing that centroid has at least 4/9 of
the total mixed volume. Zero-length endpoint fibers carry no volume and
can be discarded for this assertion. This improves 1/e only for this
vertical d=1 component; oblique cuts are not covered by this lemma.

No corresponding tail power 1/(d+1) assertion for general d is assumed
here. The square-root proof above uses the exact finite sum of an affine
sequence; replacing it by an integral would lose the delta/8 term.
